mcqs.question: Why does a CSRF token fail to protect against clickjacking?
options: The attacker's page can read the token out of the framed document
The click really happens on your page, so the request carries a valid token and your own Origin
CSRF tokens are not sent on requests originating inside an iframe
The token is invalidated when the page is loaded in a frame
mcqs.explanation: The victim clicks a genuine button in your genuinely-loaded page, so the request is indistinguishable from a legitimate one at the HTTP layer — token present, session valid, Origin naming you. The attacker never needs to read anything from the frame, which is why the same-origin policy holding does not help here.

mcqs.question: You need exactly two partner domains to be able to embed your widget. Which mechanism can express that?
options: `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM` listing both domains
`X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` plus a server-side Referer check
A `<meta http-equiv>` tag carrying `frame-ancestors`
`Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` with both origins listed
mcqs.explanation: `frame-ancestors` accepts a list of origins and wildcards, which is precisely the case it was designed for. `ALLOW-FROM` never shipped in Chrome or Safari and is deprecated, and framing directives delivered by meta tag are silently ignored by browsers — so both alternatives look right and provide nothing.

mcqs.question: An app sets a strong CSP entirely through a `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` tag, including `frame-ancestors 'none'`. What is the result?
options: The whole policy is ignored, since CSP must always be a header
The policy applies except `frame-ancestors`, which is silently ignored, leaving the page framable
The policy applies fully but only after the first paint
The browser logs a fatal error and refuses to render the document
mcqs.explanation: A meta-delivered CSP works for most fetch directives but cannot express `frame-ancestors` or `report-uri`, and the browser drops those without warning — so the framing protection appears present in the HTML and does nothing. Only a real response header can carry it.

mcqs.question: Why is JavaScript frame-busting an unreliable defense even when the script is written correctly?
options: Modern browsers deprecated the ability to inspect the top window
The script runs too early in the page lifecycle to detect the frame
Search engines penalise pages that navigate the top window
The parent can load the page in a sandboxed iframe that denies top-level navigation, so the script's action is refused
mcqs.explanation: The attacker controls the parent and can withhold the sandbox token that permits navigating the top window, so the bust script executes and its escape is simply denied — the containment feature disables the defense. Nothing about frame detection has been deprecated; the problem is that detecting the frame does not give you the power to leave it.

mcqs.question: Your app sets `frame-ancestors 'none'` in middleware and a pentest still reports clickjacking. What is the most likely cause?
options: Some HTML responses bypass the middleware — error pages, or content served directly by the CDN or a storage bucket
`frame-ancestors 'none'` only applies to same-origin frames
The middleware ordering means the header is set after the body is sent
Browsers require `X-Frame-Options` to be present for `frame-ancestors` to take effect
mcqs.explanation: Coverage gaps, not the directive, are the usual finding: anything not passing through your app — error templates, legacy routes, HTML in an assets bucket — ships without the header and remains framable. `frame-ancestors 'none'` blocks all framing including same-origin, and it is independent of the legacy header rather than dependent on it.
